title: CompleteP for RL: Scaling Without Losing What Matters
one_liner: When you make a learning machine bigger, use CompleteP (a way to scale the learning speed) to keep the learning process stable and the learned features consistent.
lead: When training deep reinforcement learning agents (machines that learn by trial and error), making them bigger sometimes backfires: the learning becomes chaotic, learned patterns shift unexpectedly, and what works for a small agent fails for a large one. This paper shows that CompleteP, a method for scaling the learning step size as the model grows, preserves stable learning and keeps the same hyperparameters working across model sizes.

paras: When you train a machine to make decisions in an environment (like a robot learning to grab objects), you nudge the model's internal numbers (called weights) by a fixed amount each time you see a mistake. As the model grows from 1 million to 100 million weights, the same nudge size causes all kinds of trouble: the learning becomes unpredictable, the learned behaviors shift erratically, and a learning speed that worked perfectly for the small model fails utterly for the large one.

A beginner might try to just double the nudge size along with the model size, but this backfires too: the learning overshoots, the model thrashes around randomly, or stops learning altogether. The core problem is that as the model gets wider (more weights doing the same job in parallel), their collective effect on the model's behavior grows, but no one adjusts for it.

callout.html: CompleteP scales the learning step size carefully so that when the model grows, the learning process stays smooth, learned patterns stay consistent, and the same learning speed works for big and small models alike.

steps.text: Count how many weights exist in each layer.
Divide the base learning rate by the square root of width.
Start weights with variance that shrinks as width grows.
Run the learning algorithm with the scaled step size.
Learning curves, learned features, and final policy remain consistent.

object.h2: What changes: the learning step size
paras: CompleteP changes one specific thing: the size of each learning nudge as the model grows. Instead of keeping it fixed or blindly scaling it up, CompleteP scales it down proportionally to the square root of the model width. This single change ripples through everything: how fast learning converges, which features the model learns, and whether the policy (the learned decision-making behavior) stays consistent.

hidden.name: Feature consistency across scales
paras: Feature consistency is a hidden quantity: how much do the internal learned patterns (the mid-layer features that represent concepts the model discovers) shift when you change the model size? In the small model, the model might learn that 'edge-direction' is useful; in the big model with naive scaling, it might learn 'color-blob' instead. CompleteP keeps the model learning the same features even as it grows, which means the learned behavior generalizes more smoothly.

The paper estimates feature consistency by measuring how similar the learned features are across model sizes, and by tracking how policy rewards stay consistent. Models trained with CompleteP show high feature overlap (the learned concepts are the same), while models trained with the NTK lazy approach drift and learn different internal representations.

heat.caption: Darker means the quantity is more present; CompleteP (highlighted) maintains consistency; NTK degrades.

reads.html: When you learn something, your brain builds new connections in a certain pattern. If you try to learn the same thing in a bigger brain (more neurons, same person), you expect the connections to form the same way, not completely differently. CompleteP makes neural networks behave this way.

The paper measures how aligned the learned patterns are (using a numerical similarity score from 0 to 1; higher is more similar) across model sizes. CompleteP agents show high similarity scores (near 1.0), meaning the learned internal patterns stay nearly identical as the model grows. NTK agents show lower scores (0.3–0.6 range) as width increases, proving their learned patterns diverge.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: balance between learning speed and model size
paras: When a layer has N parallel weights all learning from the same training signal, they combine to amplify the effect: collectively they push the model N times harder than a single weight alone. CompleteP counteracts this by dividing the learning step by the square root of N. This maintains a constant effective learning speed across model sizes.

The deeper reason: in reinforcement learning, the data distribution changes as the agent learns (it explores different states, discovers new mistakes). Under this moving target, CompleteP preserves two critical things. First, the directional nudges (which way each weight should move) stay consistent across sizes, so the model learns the same internal features regardless of width; this matters because if a small model learns to recognize 'useful action types' and a large model learns 'raw pixel colors' instead, they will behave completely differently even if both have high reward. Second, the effective learning trajectory (the path through learning space) remains stable, so training is predictable and hyperparameters do not need tuning for every new model size.

stages.s: Agent observes state and takes action
Compute error (did the action work?) and gradient (which way to nudge weights)
Scale gradient by CompleteP factor (divide by sqrt of layer width)
Update weights: move them by the scaled gradient
Learned behavior stays stable; features match other model sizes

math.h2: The scaling law: learning step shrinks with model width
symbols: learning step size for layer i
base learning step (the starting value you pick)
number of weights in layer i

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Layer with 64 weights, base learning step 0.01: actual step = 0.01 / sqrt(64) = 0.01 / 8 = 0.00125
Same layer expanded to 256 weights: actual step = 0.01 / sqrt(256) = 0.01 / 16 = 0.000625
Quadrupling width halves the step, exactly as intended: amplified collective effect is cancelled out.

math.note: The square root relationship means that the collective learning effect of many parallel weights stays constant even as the model grows, keeping the learning process stable and predictable.

items.html: If the base learning step is set too conservatively, CompleteP shrinks it further, and the model barely learns anything. You must tune the base step for the model family, not randomly guess it.

CompleteP assumes the scaling relationship holds throughout training. If the task changes (the reward structure shifts), or if the agent's exploration strategy changes dramatically, the scaling law may break down.

If you transfer hyperparameters from a small model to a large one, both must be trained with CompleteP for the transfer to work. Mixing CompleteP and naive scaling across sizes causes erratic behavior.
Choose the base learning step once for your model family, apply CompleteP to all sizes, and hyperparameters transfer cleanly without retuning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple control task (like a pendulum or cartpole that learns to swing upright). Train agents with CompleteP and without (NTK parameterization) at two sizes: 2 hidden layers of 64 units (small) and 2 hidden layers of 256 units (large). Use the same hyperparameters for both, and report: (1) final reward achieved, (2) how similar the learned features are across sizes (measure the cosine similarity of hidden layer activations), and (3) how smoothly the learning curve progresses (how much it oscillates).
demo.metric_eq: feature_consistency = mean(cosine_similarity(small_features, large_features)); reward_transfer = reward_large / reward_small
demo.closing: The key observation: CompleteP achieves feature consistency > 0.8 and reward transfer > 0.95, meaning the learned behavior and internal patterns are nearly identical across sizes. NTK parameterization shows feature consistency < 0.5 and reward transfer < 0.7, proving that learning diverges.
